constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
Any form of physical contact with others

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost Community and culture' is not impossible for a combat trauma survivor, but for a 49-year-old married male European city council member it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile and is weakly anchored to the rest of the selected nodes. The rest of the profile centers on bodily danger, touch/startle, fragmented trauma recall, and safety distrust; this item instead implies a culturally/community dislocation theme that is not supported elsewhere in Triggers/Threat/Memory/Maladaptive Strategies.

issues.item: Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
issues.explanation: 'Overwhelming grief on recall' is not inherently inconsistent, but here it is the least coherent memory item relative to the formulation and other selected items. The profile is dominated by fear-based threat, bodily vulnerability, touch alarm, and cognitive disorganization of recall. A grief-dominant recall item without corresponding loss/bereavement appraisals or related strategies makes the memory cluster less internally aligned.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The profile is largely coherent for a middle-aged male combat survivor, but this appraisal is the main mismatch. 'My body has been permanently damaged' implies a salient lasting physical injury. That idea is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile: memory items focus on fragmented, terror-laden recall; threat items emphasize current danger, mistrust of safety, startle to touch, and sleep disturbance; maladaptive strategies emphasize sensory distraction, thought monitoring, and avoidance of touch. There are no triggers selected, and no other items indicate ongoing medical consequences or trauma themes centered on bodily injury. In this profile, the appraisal reads as if it belongs to a different subtype centered on physical injury rather than the represented combat-related fear/terror formulation.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile in a 49-year-old male, this specific self-blame item is the main coherence problem. The rest of the profile centers on persistent danger, touch-triggered alarm, fragmented/terror-laden memory, and defensive avoidance, which fits combat-related PTSD. In contrast, 'the event happened because of the way I acted' implies a strong internal-causal guilt formulation that is not otherwise supported by the selected memory, threat, or strategy items. This makes the appraisal set less coherent with the overall profile and with the formulation, where Memory and Threat strongly feed Negative Appraisals focused on ongoing danger rather than responsibility for causing the trauma. Self-blame can occur in combat PTSD, but here it is insufficiently connected to the other selected items and stands out as the least clinically coherent item.

vignette: Julian Vance was forty-two when the ambush split his convoy in the highlands. The initial blast erased the seconds that followed, leaving only a fractured sequence of shouting, the sharp tang of cordite, and hands hauling him through mud and shattered vehicle glass. He remembered the weight of a comrade’s grip on his shoulder, the sudden, jarring contact that had yanked him clear, and the chaotic sweep of movement that followed. The rest of the deployment was a blank space, a silence where hours should have been. He had come to believe that the missing pieces were gone forever, swallowed by the violence. When Julian returned to his city council office in the capital, the quiet of his study felt heavier than the noise had. He was certain that if he let his guard down, the chaos would follow him through the door. He found himself constantly scanning the room for exits, his neck tight, his eyes fixed on every shift of light and shadow. He had come to believe the world was a dangerous place, and his body was a traitor that refused to accept the ceasefire. Every time his pulse quickened or his muscles coiled without warning, he knew his physiology was still bracing for an attack that had ended years ago. Sleep became a foreign concept. He lay awake, tracking the creak of the house and the shadows against the ceiling, unable to fall or stay asleep. Even when his wife or colleagues assured him he was home, he found it impossible to believe it. The words landed like stones in water; they sank without leaving a ripple of reassurance. Over the next year, a rigid routine solidified. He turned on the television or blasted heavy music until the speakers hummed, just to keep the quiet from crowding his mind. He spent hours monitoring his own thoughts, listening for any drift toward panic or disorientation, convinced that losing that internal surveillance meant he was unraveling. He learned to avoid being touched by anyone. When Elena reached to steady him as he rose from his desk, Julian flinched violently, his breath catching in sharp alarm. He had come to believe that any unexpected contact was a prelude to the highlands. Handshakes at donor events became a negotiation of angles; a colleague’s hand on his back during a committee meeting sent his heart hammering against his ribs. He stopped attending the public forums altogether, telling constituents he was recovering from surgery. The gaps in his recollection made it impossible to speak about the deployment. When Elena asked what he had been through, Julian would open his mouth, but he would lose the thread. He could not explain what happened clearly, and each time the panic rose, he retreated further. Remembering the event brought back the same terror he had felt at the time, a familiar, suffocating heat that drowned out his words. By his forty-ninth year, the distance between him and his council duties had become a chasm. He missed the late-night debates, the quiet camaraderie with his staff, the simple rhythm of public service. What finally brought him through the clinic’s doors was a collapsed evening in the council chambers. A junior aide had placed a reassuring hand on his shoulder during a recess, and Julian had stumbled backward, knocking over a stack of reports, his breath coming in ragged gasps. He had seen the confusion on the aide’s face, then the quiet worry in Elena’s eyes when he returned home. Julian sat in the waiting room now, his hands folded tightly in his lap, bracing for the intake nurse to approach. He hoped to find a way to stop his body from treating every normal moment as a threat. He was terrified of losing his marriage, of becoming the man who had lost his own mind, but he was equally terrified of what would happen if he never learned to step off the perimeter. He just wanted the noise in his head to settle enough to hear himself again.
